title: You can make this DIY controller in six hours and for less than 12 bucks—but would you want to?
summary: I think I'll stick with my GameSir Nova Lite.
body: In my past life as a console gamer, I was wary of any controller not bundled in with my first-party hardware. These days though, there are lots of excellent PC gamepad options—particularly in the budget category—but how cheap is too cheap? Our current pick for the best PC controller that won't hurt your wallet is the GameSir Nova Lite . This costs comfortably under $30 on a good day, but how low can you go in the budget realm? Well, how about a pad you can make yourself in about six hours for €10 (or about $11.22)? The catch is… uh, well, just look at it . Dubbed the Undercooked V0.4, this thing doesn't have a D-pad or even a full set of face buttons. Instead, this project limits itself to a single analogue stick, 'X' and 'A' inputs, a menu button, and a 'B' button that's been relegated to the pad's right shoulder. According to the creator, Lazy_Duck, "the idea was to make it simple, affordable and that you could get all components even in the smallest electronics shop quick and cheap." As such, this simplified pad doesn't even feature a full PCB. Instead, you'll need a protoboard with an RP2040-Zero microcontroller—that is, if you fancy DIY-ing something that looks a bit like the…

title: GameSir Nova Lite 2 review
summary: The best deal in controllers at $30 or less right now.
body: The GameSir Nova Lite 2 is our new best budget controller for PC. It's extremely well equipped considering the small asking price. Depart with just $30 / £30 of your hard-earned cash, and you'll receive a wireless controller with Hall effect sticks, mechanical D-pad, trigger stops, and programmable rear buttons. There's enough here that even GameSir's own exceedingly popular G7 Pro is at risk of cannibalisation. The Nova Lite 2 doesn't look that out of shape by comparison, with only quality of life and more advanced features between them. Such as a handful of micro switches and a bigger battery. The G7 Pro is a better all-round controller, but for less than half the cash, the Nova Lite 2 is tough to ignore. There are some drawbacks with a controller at this price. The plastic doesn't feel great and it's not overly grippy. The software could be smarter and the shoulder buttons wider, too. But they all seem savvy sacrifices for the savings that the Nova Lite 2 delivers. Buy if... ✅ You don't use a controller often and you're not looking to spend a lot of money: If you use a mouse and keyboard for most of your gaming, you don't need the next best thing. title: PS5-exclusive Demon's Souls Remake not only runs on PC now, it's running at twice the fps cap on an RTX 5070 with frame gen
summary: It could be smoother but double the frames is nothing to sniff at.
body: As a console gaming interloper, I've been watching the PlayStation 5 emulation scene from afar with some interest. The latest development to catch my eye is that emulation of the Demon's Souls Remake, which has been exclusive to Sony's console since its 2020 launch, can now run at up to 120 fps on PC. Leveraging the very much unofficial KytyPS5 translation layer, YouTuber Geralt Benchmarks shared footage of the remake running on their RTX 5070 and AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D rig. The game reaches for more than 100 fps at 1440p resolution thanks to 2x DLSS frame generation, and you can watch it achieve a mostly buttery 120 fps at 1080p at the eight minute mark here . Otherwise on Sony's hardware, the game is locked to 60 fps and 1440p resolution while in performance mode. Doubling the frames via emulation is impressive to say the least, especially for what is still a current-gen console. For the sake of comparison, Geralt Benchmarks also shows the game running on their RTX 5070 rig with those PS5 settings left in place, turning in a performance that occasionally crests over the 70 fps mark. This emulated version isn't without its quirks, though. Even in Geralt Benchmarks' footage, there's …

title: No publishers wanted Outlast because they'd 'rather invest $50,000 in 10 mobile games' so Red Barrels relied on public investment programs and their own savings instead
summary: "Everything was on the line" during Outlast's development.
body: Outlast has long since established itself as a horror gaming staple with an impressive track record of two mainline games, a DLC, and an online multiplayer game that still scares the bejesus out of me. So it's hard to believe that there was a time when developer Red Barrels was unsure whether or not it'd even be able to get it out of the door. After trying and failing to convince Ubisoft to let him make a horror game and just generally feeling like it was time to move on, Philippe Morin, co-founder of Red Barrels decided to leave and form a small 10-person team with developers from other big-budget studios. Their first pitch: a horror game. (Image credit: Red Barrels) “We thought at first that we’d come up with the pitch within three or four months and shop it around to a few publishers," Morin says in an interview with GameSpot . "And we’d find out pretty quickly if it works or not." Unfortunately, it turned out to be the latter, at least at first. Morin explains how many of the publishers they approached would “rather invest $50,000 in 10 mobile games than $500,000 in [Outlast].” This was likely equal parts because of how obsessed everyone was with mobile games back then and tha…

summary: All the interesting Steam facts for the week ending October 18.
body: We are drowning in shit. Steam Next Fest, which kicks off tomorrow, currently has 8,011 matches on its press preview landing page. That's roughly double the amount of demos featured in Steam's June 2026 Next Fest. In June 2022, Next Fest boasted just over a thousand demos. The vast majority of these demos will be meritless slop. And I daresay many of them—though I have no way to confirm—didn't exist as concepts before October. If you use social media, especially X, you've probably noticed an explosion of terrible clones and vibe coded mash-ups this month. You can largely thank Anthropic's new 5.5 update to its Claude Opus model for that, which offers massive efficiency gains for vibe coders. It's also been widely used to decompile commercial games and, maybe most famously, jailbreak the PS5. It definitely feels like we've crossed a threshold this month. On October 10, the creator of Escape the Walls , an incremental punching game which itself uses AI to "increase the speed of creating the game", posted in-progress footage from the game on X . title: Dark Souls 2 dataminer shows off massive prototype coliseum level from early development
summary: Bigger than the ones in Elden Ring, for what it's worth.
body: At a glance The rough prototype looks to have been binned early in development, and it's largely avoided discussion before Doneda's work. Some portions appear to have been part of an interconnected area, others are likely different versions of the same concept. It may have been related to what became the Undead Crypt in the final game. Doneda uses Elden Ring Nightreign to load in and explore what remains of the levels. The files contain a coliseum zone, mines, a strange underground tower (potentially a sequence of arenas, like Nightreign's DLC?), and a crypt portion. Doneda , the dataminer who showed off the unused levels, has been proving a genuine authority on Dark Souls 2 in particular. Previously, they made a Nightreign-compatible version of Dark Souls 2's Eleum Loyce . Doneda has also shown off a tantalizingly ambitious early version of Dark Souls 2's The Gutter. In hindsight, the entire pre-Sekiro Souls series (perhaps sans-Bloodborne) seems defined by difficult, rushed development cycles. title: The Outlast Trials' initial playtests went poorly: Designer says 6-year development took 'a f**king long time' and 'a s**t-ton of prototypes'
summary: Red Barrels co-founder Philippe Morin recently spoke on the trials The Outlast Trials outlasted.
body: Gamedev may as well be conducted in a black box as far as many players are concerned, so it can be easy to think of a good game as one where development went smoothly and a bad game as one where things went terribly awry. But in the case of The Outlast Trials, making something sickeningly good took a lot of struggle. As Red Barrels co-founder Philippe Morin told Gamespot in a recent interview , it took six years to turn the vague notion of a co-op Outlast game into something ready to launch via early access. It was "a fucking long time," as he recalled it, and the product of "a shit-ton of prototypes." "[The Red Barrels team] went too far trying to make [The Outlast Trials] systemic, random, and trying to reach our ultimate goal of infinite replayability," he told Gamespot. "We needed to come back to something that maybe added less replayability, but definitely felt more like Outlast." The article notes that a seemingly shippable build was produced within four years, but playtests went poorly enough to send the team back to the drawing board. I suppose concerns about replayability have been put to rest now that it's mutated into a sizable live service game with around 20,000 peopl…

title: No soundtrack does it like Hades 2
summary: I'm still listening to this thing a year later.
body: Critical Hit (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Critical Hit , where I (or someone else on the PC Gamer team) celebrate and lament all things videogame music, audio design, and the ways our favourite games make our ears tingle. I have not played Hades 2 since October 4 of 2025. That's not because I "fell out of love" with the game or whatever, I simply plugged 65 hours into it, beat the 'main story', had a jolly old time, and went on to play other things. But one thing about it has persisted: its soundtrack. God, I can't get Hades 2's soundtrack out of my head. I'm going to outline some of my favorites, but before I do that, I do want to give flowers to the more ambient tunes on Darren Korb's masterwork, here. Edge of Erebus, Spider Silk, and particularly The Song of Sirens—perhaps the most faithful rendition of their mythological namesake before Korb, genius that he is, clubs you over the head with a rock band. What really cements Hades 2's soundtrack in my mind, however, are its show-stoppers. These boss themes are the real events, so much so that Korb will often bring in a guest musician to set the track on fire. Scylla and the Sirens' Discography The entire collection of Scylla…

body: Disk Cleanup (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?" Joe Ziegler might be best known for his role guiding the design of big competitive shooters, but his formative gaming experiences were with point-and-click adventures like King's Quest. "There was something so clever about trying to use all this knowledge about random things like fairy tales to try to solve puzzles inside of the game," he says. "It was just that 'A-ha!' moment where videogames could be these really engaging ways for you to be clever and creative." Ziegler started out at Pandemic Studios, where he worked as a mission designer on 2009's The Saboteur. But he is best known as game director on Riot's hugely popular arena shooter Valorant , and his more recent oversight of Bungie's extraction-shooter revival of Marathon , which he assumed leadership of in March 2024 following the dismissal of former director Christopher Barret . title: Outlast designer says that one playtester was so upset by the horror series they 'ran out of the studio to go cry outside' and didn't return
summary: "We always make sure that people are fully aware of the kind of content we create," says director Philippe Morin.
body: Red Barrels' Outlast series has long held a reputation for pushing the envelope further than most horror games, with depictions of violence, gore and nudity that can be shocking even within a medium well versed in delivering scares. But it isn't just audiences who have found the studio's games shocking beyond the virtual horror norm. As co-founder Phillipe Morin recently revealed, there have been numerous instances where people in and around the studio have found working with the material frightening to the point of being traumatic. In a chat with Gamespot , Morin discussed the studio's unflinching approach to horror, explaining that it wasn't a deliberate attempt to court controversy, and was simply a "personal preference" on Morin and the other co-founders' behalf. "We didn't start like 'Oh, we've got to make the goriest game out there'" Morin explained. "It was just, 'we're making a horror game, so obviously we'll make it gory. I remember even the scriptwriter early on was saying, 'There's never too much blood.'" Nonetheless, the intense and graphic nature of Outlast' horror has proved triggering within the studio. title: Discussion time: Do you think zone chats in MMOs are forces for good, or evil?
summary: What's up, Barrens Chat.
body: Terminally Online (Image credit: Future) This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice. Ah, zone chats in MMOs—trade and general chats, /shouts and /yells. Intended as a way to render the social glue that binds these videogames together, they are often instead a tableau for (and I say this somewhat affectionately) absolute lunacy, pock-marked with some of the most vile verbiage you'll see online. Take, for instance, the time-honoured tradition of "Barrens Chat" in World of Warcraft. Combine a big zone that spans around 10-15 levels along with proximity to a major city, and you get a certain kind of verbal hooliganry that, in my journeys through WoW: Forever, I was actually pretty nostalgic for. I mean, sure, the Chuck Norris jokes have gotten a smidge old. But while collecting Zhevra Hoofs, I would find myself possessed to ask Barrens Chat philosophical questions, and while I never received much in the way of wisdom, responses wer…

title: Ghostwire: Tokyo joins GOG Preservation Program, which means you don't have to deal with Bethesda.NET anymore
summary: …if you get it on GOG, anyway.
body: Ghostwire: Tokyo, Tango Gameworks' spooky, neon-drenched action-adventure game, is now officially a good old game. Granted, it's not that old, but 'good' seems about right given that contributing writer Imogen Mellor scored it a 72 in her review . But what I mean is that it's joined GOG's Preservation Program . If you're wondering why a game from 2022 would need to be preserved already, well, it kind of doesn't. You may be thinking the game is finally free from its seemingly arbitrary implementation of Denuvo , but that was actually removed shortly after it was added . What this release does is remove Bethesda.NET integration (providing any extra goodies on your first launch of the game) and come with a promise from GOG that any stability issues that arise as decades pass and operating systems change will be addressed in future patches. That may just come into play given that Tango Gameworks would be closed right now if Xbox's sudden closure of the studio hadn't been canceled out with an acquisition by PUBG owner Krafton . It's worth noting that the game still appears to be published by Bethesda Softworks, so if you're trying to avoid Microsoft products for any genocide-related re…

title: The Cyberpunk 2077 movie won't be 'a film adaptation of the game,' CD Projekt chief says
summary: The game is great, but CD Projekt wants to tell a new story.
body: We learned last week that a Cyberpunk 2077 movie is in the works , an announcement I used mainly to talk about a completely different cyberpunk movie starring Keanu Reeves as a guy named Johnny who's having a bad week. Now we've got a bit more insight into what CD Projekt Red has in mind for the film, and it's possible that a guy named Johnny may not be involved at all. "Our contract with Anonymous Content expired, and in the meantime, an opportunity arose to establish cooperation with Paramount Pictures," co-CEO Michał Nowakowski told Polish PAP Biznes ( Google translated ), referring to the Cyberpunk 2077 "live action project" that was announced in 2023 and ultimately went nowhere. "We decided that we would conduct a live-action Cyberpunk project in a new formula. "At this point, we can only say that we definitely don't want to make a film adaptation of the game. We want to tell a story in the world of Cyberpunk, but it won't be a one-to-one translation of the game's story." I loved Cyberpunk 2077, and the fact that it featured two Hollywood stars in central roles might make it seem like a natural fit for a direct translation. But I think avoiding that approach is the wiser move…

title: 'We f**ked up': 1 day into Wardogs Season 2, the Blue team bribery bonus is being dropped
summary: Bulkhead's effort to make life better for the Blues worked a little too well.
body: One day into Wardogs Season 2, Bulkhead Interactive has decided to scrap the bribery plan it announced last week as a way to help convince players to join the Blue team. The problem isn't that the plan didn't work—it actually worked far too well. THE PLAN: "Lonestar cash and XP bonus. Season 2 only. New Bakurani spawn." "We're looking at how we can help the win rate of a certain team." -Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer (via "Road to Season 2" devlog) THE REALITY: "We were wrong. We fucked up," Brammer admitted in a new video (via RPS). Blue team is now winning "by far, the most," Brammer said, even though the actual boosts are not terribly substantial: 5% Lonestar cash and 2.5% XP. "Median" players didn't get much from those percentages, but Bulkhead found that "top tier" players were seeing significant boosts Bottom line: it's gone. "We're removing the Blue XP bonus, the cash bonus. We were wrong," Brammer said. Bulkhead co-founder Howard Philpott added that the studio thought Blue team bonus might work out this way, but said "I don't think we expected it to be this much of a swing." title: Less than 2 weeks after announcing RuneScape Reignited, Jagex is scrapping the whole thing
summary: In the wake of a furious backlash from players, Jagex admits it "missed the mark."
body: Life comes at you fast, as the saying goes, and the folks at RuneScape developer Jagex can sure attest to that. Less than two weeks after announcing RuneScape Reignited —essentially a way for new and lapsed players to restart their adventures from fresh on separate, unique servers—the studio has decided to cancel it. There was trouble with RuneScape Reignited almost right from the start, with complaints ranging from a potential community split to restrictions on character interactions and the need to pay for a separate subscription. Just a few days after the initial announcement, Jagex apologized for making veteran players feel like they were being shunted aside, and said it was "exploring a heavy set of revisions to Reignited based on your feedback." A few days after that, it laid out a more specific list of intended alterations , and invited more feedback from players, "so we can follow up next week with more of our thoughts." With that feedback now received, it seems that Jagex has heard enough. "It is clear that we missed the mark on this, and so we are not moving forward with it," Mod Ryan—associate creative director Ryan Philpott—said in a blog post announcing the cancellati…

title: Street Fighter review roundup: sorry, folks, but it sounds like a mess
summary: The general consensus seems to be that Street Fighter isn't a disaster, but it definitely misses a lot more than it hits.
body: I had such high hopes for the Street Fighter movie: The trailers were so promising, the cast so charismatic, and it seemed to get the inherent ridiculousness of the franchise, playing it seriously without ever really taking it too seriously. I mean, you don't put a guy like David Dastmalchian in the role of M. Bison unless you expect him to do something with it, right? Alas, it seems that this may be a real Tuesday , at least for my Street Fighter movie aspirations. The reviews are in, and they are not especially kind. Street Fighter isn't a complete catastrophe, according to the critical consensus, but I don't think JCVD has to worry about having to turn in his "Best Street Fighter Movie" trophy anytime soon, either. title: World of Warcraft: Forever devs say gear upgrades will stay relevant 'for a long, long time': 'It's very much our intention to try wherever we can to not invalidate old content'
summary: Blizzard says items won't work like the modern version of the MMO.
body: The developers of World of Warcraft: Forever, the venerable MMO's newest 'Classic+' flavor, say that even though the level cap is staying at 60, there will always be new gear to chase, and lower level gear has never been more powerful. Blizzard Entertainment developers are wary of the drastic increases in power in WoW's modern version, including the recent Midnight expansion, which render previous seasons of gear irrelevant, require massive resets between expansions and lead to periodic stat "squishes" to avoid players becoming omnipotent gods. "Classic wasn't far off from this," vice president and senior game director Ion Hazzikostas said of Forever's approach in a recent PC Gamer interview. "It's gradual. Going from [Classic raids] Blackwing Lair to Ahn'Qiraj that's actually only a couple of item levels higher. Those two largely coexist. C'thun drops are probably better than anything in Blackwing Lair, but that's like one or two items per player. This is a system that can last for a long, long time."
